body:
Fixes #6120.

## Problem

For error messages (`last read: '...'`), the lexer keeps the text of the token it is reading. The token start moves only at strings and numbers, so after a string or number everything that follows (whitespace, structural characters, literals) still belongs to that token. Input that cannot be read again copies it while parsing: the `std::istream` and `FILE*` adapters in their carry buffer on every buffer refill, and the lexer in `token_string` for iterator and other input. Valid input such as `1` followed by 100,000,000 newlines therefore peaked at about 225 MB for `std::istream`, `FILE*` and input iterators (3.12.0: the same), and the raw text of a long string was kept a second time next to the parsed value.

## Change

The text is only used for error messages, so it does not need to be kept in full:

- `token_text_buffer<CharType>` (in `input_adapters.hpp`, outside the `JSON_NO_IO` guard) replaces the char-only `token_carry_buffer` (now an alias of `token_text_buffer<char>`) and the lexer's `std::vector<char_type> token_string`. It keeps the first 4096 and at least the last 4112 characters of a token. When it is full and holds more than 12,320 characters, it drops the characters in between instead of growing. That happens in `make_room()`, the out-of-line path that previously reallocated, so appending a character is still one comparison and a store. The capacity never exceeds 12,320 characters.
- `get_token_string()` shows a token of more than 8192 characters as its first 4096 characters, `...`, and its last 4096 characters. For contiguous input, which rebuilds the token from positions, it copies only these two parts instead of the whole range.
- `exceptions.md` (parse_error.101) describes the shortened token.

Tokens of up to 8192 characters are shown exactly as before. Messages for longer tokens are the same for every kind of input; the test below checks this for `std::string`, `std::istream`, `FILE*` and `std::list<char>`.

## Measurements

Peak resident memory for valid input of `1` followed by 100,000,000 newlines (reproducer in #6120, Apple clang 21 `-O2`):

| input | develop | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| `std::istream` | 224.8 MB | 1.8 MB |
| `FILE*` | 225.3 MB | 1.8 MB |
| input iterator | 225.3 MB | 1.7 MB |

The same input with a `?` at the end (a parse error) peaks at 2.4 to 2.7 MB, and its `what()` has 65,684 bytes for all three inputs.

Parsing speed, instructions retired (develop vs. this PR, 20 parses each; `std::list<char>` 5), Apple clang 21 `-O2 -DNDEBUG`, arm64:

| input | canada | citm_catalog | twitter |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `std::string` | -0.06 % | +0.02 % | -0.12 % |
| `std::istream` | +0.03 % | -0.08 % | +0.06 % |
| `FILE*` | -0.03 % | -0.07 % | -0.01 % |
| `std::list<char>` | -16.97 % | -12.89 % | -14.11 % |

The iterator path gets cheaper because the buffer's `push_back` does less than `std::vector::push_back`. A first version that kept `std::vector` and added a capacity check before each character cost +5 % to +22 % there, so it was dropped.

On Linux (GCC 15.2, `-O2 -DNDEBUG`, x86-64), exact instruction counts with callgrind (3 parses each):

| input | canada | citm_catalog | twitter |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `std::string` | +39 | −42 | −5 |
| `std::istream` | +92 | +105 | +99 |
| `FILE*` | −3,175 | −2,247 | −657 |
| `std::list<char>` | −4.42 % | −3.19 % | −1.11 % |

(for `std::string`, `std::istream` and `FILE*` these are instructions out of 70 to 420 million, i.e. below 0.001 %). Wall times on the same machine varied by ±4 % in both directions between identical builds, so they are not given.

## Tests

- `unit-class_lexer.cpp`: `token_text_buffer` directly, with characters added one by one and in pieces of different sizes (around the 4112-character boundary and larger than the capacity): the first 4096 and the last 4112 characters are kept, the size stays within the limit, `pop_back()` after dropping works, and `clear()` starts a new token.
- `unit-class_parser.cpp`: the message of a long string, of a long whitespace run after a number, and of a token just below the limit, each for `std::string`, `std::istream`, `FILE*` (tmpfile) and `std::list<char>`; valid input with a long whitespace run. 8 of its assertions fail on develop.
- With ASan and UBSan, C++11 and C++20: class_parser, class_lexer, stream-bulk-scan, file_input, user_defined_input, deserialization, wstring, diagnostics, diagnostic-positions, guard-page, precise-stream-position, ubjson, bjdata, contiguous_parser, testsuites, unicode, alt-string, noexcept, regression1, regression2, json_view. It also builds with `JSON_NO_IO` (C++11 `-O0`) and with GCC 16 without warnings. clang-tidy (CI configuration) is clean.

## Breaking changes

No API change. The text of a parse error message changes for a token of more than 8192 characters: the middle of the token is replaced by `...`. The SAX `parse_error()` `last_token` argument is shortened in the same way. Message texts are not part of the API.
